topic.subject: English
topic.name: Grammar Terms: Pronouns and Determiners
topic.description: Know and use Year 4 grammar terminology including determiner, pronoun, possessive pronoun, and adverbial

Explain the difference between a possessive pronoun ('mine', 'theirs') and other pronouns ('I', 'they')
Use the terms 'determiner' and 'adverbial' accurately when discussing a classmate's writing

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Modal Verbs and Possibility
topic.description: Understand and use modal verbs (can, may, must, might, shall, will, could, should, would) and modal adverbs (perhaps, surely, certainly) to indicate degrees of possibility, necessity, and permission
evidence: Select a modal verb to express certainty, probability, or possibility in a sentence, e.g. 'It will rain' vs 'It might rain' vs 'It could rain'
Replace a modal verb with a modal adverb to achieve a similar effect, e.g. 'He might come' → 'Perhaps he will come'
Distinguish between modals expressing permission (may, can), obligation (must, should), and possibility (might, could) in context
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes, do they choose between words like "must", "might", "could", and "should" to show whether something is certain, possible, or just an idea — rather than treating every action as definite?

prerequisites.reason: Modal verbs modify main verbs to express possibility/necessity; learners need a secure grasp of simple verb tenses before adding modal modifiers
prerequisites.name: Simple Past, Present and Future

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Plural vs Possessive in Nouns
topic.description: Distinguish between the plural -s suffix and the possessive -'s suffix in nouns
evidence: Sort words like 'dogs', 'dog's', and 'dogs'' into plural, singular possessive, and plural possessive categories
Explain why 'the cats bowl' is incorrect and supply the correct form ('the cat's bowl' or 'the cats' bowl') for a given meaning
Write two sentences using the same noun — one as a plural and one as a possessive
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell the difference between "the girls' coats" (belonging to many girls) and "the girls are coming" (just a plural) — and write each one correctly without mixing up the apostrophe?

prerequisites.reason: Distinguishing plural -s from possessive -'s requires understanding of regular plurals

prerequisites.reason: Distinguishing plural -s from possessive 's requires prior knowledge of how apostrophes mark possession
prerequisites.name: Apostrophes: Contraction and Possession

prerequisites.reason: Builds on singular possessive apostrophe to contrast with plural -s
prerequisites.name: Apostrophes for possession

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Standard English Verbs
topic.description: Use Standard English verb inflections in place of non-standard local forms
evidence: Correct 'we was playing' to 'we were playing' and explain why the standard form is needed in writing
Choose the standard form in pairs such as 'I did / I done', 'she has / she have', 'they were / they was'
Rewrite a short passage replacing three non-standard verb forms with their Standard English equivalents
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sometimes says "we was" or "they done it" in conversation, do they know to write "we were" and "they did it" in their schoolwork — using standard written English?

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Adjective Order in Sentences
topic.description: Order adjectives within sentences according to conventional English patterns (opinion-size-age-shape-colour-origin-material-purpose) to produce natural-sounding descriptions
evidence: Arrange multiple adjectives before a noun in conventional order, e.g. 'a lovely little old rectangular green French silver whittling knife' simplified to classroom examples like 'a small red bag' not 'a red small bag'
Identify when adjective order sounds unnatural and rearrange to match English conventions, e.g. correct 'the wooden big table' to 'the big wooden table'
Apply the size-before-colour-before-material pattern in descriptive writing, e.g. 'a tall grey stone castle' rather than 'a stone grey tall castle'
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} uses several describing words together — like "a tiny old wooden box" — does the order sound natural, or do they mix up the adjectives so it sounds odd?

prerequisites.reason: Ordering multiple adjectives by conventional pattern builds on the foundational skill of using expanded noun phrases
prerequisites.name: Expanded noun phrases

prerequisites.reason: Ordering adjectives within expanded noun phrases requires prior facility with expanding NPs using modifiers
prerequisites.name: Expanded noun phrases (age 8+)

prerequisites.reason: Correctly ordering adjectives is enriched by the prior distinction between adjectives (modifying nouns) and adverbs (modifying verbs)
prerequisites.name: Adjectives vs adverbs

prerequisites.reason: Adjective order requires familiarity with adjective types; comparative/superlative work establishes adjective awareness

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Brackets and dashes for parenthesis
topic.description: Use brackets, dashes, and commas to indicate parenthesis — additional information inserted into a sentence that could be removed without changing the sentence's core meaning
evidence: Insert a parenthetical phrase using paired brackets, e.g. 'The oldest building (built in 1642) stands in the town square'
Use paired dashes to add an aside or extra detail within a sentence, e.g. 'My brother — who is older than me — lives in London'
Choose between brackets, dashes, and commas for parenthesis based on how much emphasis the aside should receive, recognising that dashes give most prominence and brackets give least
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} adds a little extra detail inside a sentence — like "The teacher, who is very strict, gave us homework" — do they correctly use brackets, dashes, or commas around that added bit?

prerequisites.reason: Direct speech punctuation introduces the concept of embedding one structure within another; parenthesis similarly embeds additional information
prerequisites.name: Punctuating Direct Speech

prerequisites.reason: Parenthetical commas are a new comma use; learners need secure comma-in-lists knowledge before learning commas for parenthesis
prerequisites.name: Commas in lists

dependents.reason: Parenthetical punctuation extends KS2 brackets, dashes, commas for parenthesis

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Capitals for proper adjectives
topic.description: Use a capital letter for adjectives formed from proper nouns, as in "We waved the Canadian flag and ate Japanese food beside a Victorian house", explain which proper noun each adjective comes from, and tell proper adjectives apart from common adjectives in the same phrase.
evidence: Capitalises adjectives formed from proper nouns in own writing (e.g. "the Canadian flag", "Japanese food")
Corrects a sentence with lowercase proper adjectives and explains which proper noun each adjective comes from (e.g. Victorian from Queen Victoria)
In a phrase such as "the tall Canadian athlete", sorts the adjectives into proper and common and capitalises only the proper one
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes about "the canadian flag" or "japanese food", do they know to use a capital letter because each word comes from the name of a country?

prerequisites.reason: Knowing that adjectives describe nouns supports sorting proper from common adjectives
prerequisites.name: Expanded noun phrases

prerequisites.reason: Knowing the term "adjective" helps the child explain the rule
prerequisites.name: Grammar Terms: Nouns, Verbs and Tense

prerequisites.reason: Capitalising proper names helps explain why a derived adjective keeps the capital
prerequisites.name: Capitals for Names, Days and I

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Cohesion within paragraphs
topic.description: Use cohesive devices within a paragraph — including pronouns, adverbials (then, after that, firstly), and synonyms — to link sentences and build a coherent flow of ideas
evidence: Replace repeated nouns with pronouns or synonyms to maintain cohesion without ambiguity, e.g. 'The explorer found a cave. She examined it carefully'
Use adverbials of sequence (firstly, then, next, finally) and cause (therefore, as a result, consequently) to connect ideas within a paragraph
Identify where cohesion breaks down in a paragraph and insert appropriate linking devices to improve the flow
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a paragraph, do the sentences flow together smoothly — using words like "however", "after this", or "in contrast" to link ideas, rather than every sentence starting with "And then"?

prerequisites.reason: Pronoun cohesion is a key cohesive device; prior work on choosing pronouns for clarity feeds directly into paragraph-level cohesion
prerequisites.name: Pronouns for clarity

prerequisites.reason: Cohesion within paragraphs requires paragraphing knowledge; learners must organise text into paragraphs before learning to build cohesion within them
prerequisites.name: Organising Writing into Paragraphs

dependents.reason: Extended cohesive devices builds on cohesion within paragraphs
dependents.name: Paragraph Cohesion

dependents.reason: Text-level cohesion extends KS2 cohesive devices within paragraphs
dependents.name: Cohesion and Transitions Across Writing

dependents.reason: Linking across paragraphs builds on within-paragraph cohesion; learners must achieve cohesion within paragraphs before linking between them

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Commas Before Joining Words
topic.description: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so, yet) when joining two independent clauses in a compound sentence
evidence: Place a comma before the coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence, e.g. 'I wanted to go outside, but it was raining'
Distinguish compound sentences (two independent clauses) from simple sentences with compound predicates, e.g. 'She sang and danced' needs no comma but 'She sang a song, and he played the piano' does
Edit writing to insert missing commas before coordinating conjunctions in compound sentences
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} joins two complete thoughts with a word like "but" or "so" — like "I wanted to go, but it was raining" — do they put a comma before that joining word?

prerequisites.reason: Comma before coordinating conjunction builds on existing comma knowledge from list commas

prerequisites.reason: Learners must understand coordinating conjunctions joining clauses before learning the punctuation rule for compound sentences
prerequisites.name: Subordinate clauses

dependents.reason: Clause boundary punctuation builds on comma use with conjunctions
dependents.name: Punctuating Clauses

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Commas to avoid ambiguity
topic.description: Use commas to clarify meaning and avoid ambiguity in sentences where the absence of a comma could cause misreading
evidence: Insert a comma to prevent ambiguity, e.g. 'Let's eat, Grandma' vs 'Let's eat Grandma' or 'Most of the time, travellers worry about their bags'
Identify sentences where a missing comma changes the meaning and explain the two possible readings
Use commas after introductory elements (adverbial phrases, subordinate clauses) to prevent misreading of the main clause
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why "Let's eat, Grandma" and "Let's eat Grandma" mean very different things — and use that kind of comma in their own writing to avoid confusion?

prerequisites.name: Commas in lists

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Commas with yes, no, and names
topic.description: Use commas to set off the words yes and no, to set off tag questions, and to indicate direct address in sentences
evidence: Write sentences using commas with yes and no at the beginning such as 'Yes, I understand'
Punctuate tag questions correctly such as 'It's cold today, isn't it?'
Use commas to set off names in direct address such as 'Sarah, please pass the salt'
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes dialogue or a letter and addresses someone by name — like "Yes, Mum, I did tidy my room" — do they use commas correctly around the name and around words like "yes" or "no"?

prerequisites.reason: Tag questions and direct address relate to dialogue punctuation

prerequisites.reason: Commas for tag questions and direct address extend the range of comma conventions beyond list use

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Converting Words into Verbs
topic.description: Convert nouns and adjectives into verbs by adding suffixes -ate, -ise (-ize), and -ify, understanding how word class changes affect sentence construction
evidence: Add -ate, -ise, or -ify to nouns or adjectives to form verbs, e.g. pollen → pollinate, advert → advertise, simple → simplify
Choose the correct verb-forming suffix for a given root and use the resulting verb in a sentence, e.g. 'They needed to classify the animals' from 'class'
Identify the word-class change when a suffix converts a noun or adjective into a verb and explain how this affects the sentence structure

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Expanded noun phrases (age 9+)

topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes directions or descriptions of a place — like "behind the old tree" or "near the top of the hill" — do they use prepositional phrases naturally to show where or when something is?

prerequisites.reason: Fronted adverbials often contain prepositional phrases; prior work with adverbials builds awareness of how preposition phrases function in sentences

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Fixing Fragments & Run-Ons
topic.description: Recognise and correct sentence fragments (incomplete sentences lacking a subject or predicate) and run-on sentences (two or more independent clauses joined without proper punctuation or conjunctions)
evidence: Identify a sentence fragment by checking whether it has both a subject and a predicate, e.g. recognise 'Running through the park' as a fragment and correct to 'The dog was running through the park'

Identify a run-on sentence where two independent clauses are fused without punctuation or a conjunction, e.g. 'I like cats I also like dogs' and correct using a full stop, comma + conjunction, or semicolon
Edit a paragraph to fix fragments and run-ons, choosing the most effective correction strategy for each error
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s writing has a sentence like "Running down the street." or two ideas jammed together without any punctuation, can they spot that something's wrong and fix it?

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Grammar Terms: Modal Verbs and Clauses
topic.description: Know and use Year 5 grammar terminology accurately when discussing reading and writing: modal verb, relative pronoun, relative clause, parenthesis, bracket, dash, cohesion, ambiguity
evidence: Label a relative clause in a sentence and identify the relative pronoun that introduces it, using correct terminology
Explain why a pair of brackets or dashes creates a parenthesis and describe its function using the term 'parenthesis'
Use the terms 'modal verb', 'cohesion', and 'ambiguity' when discussing how a writer has achieved particular effects in a text

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Linking paragraphs with adverbials
topic.description: Link ideas across paragraphs using adverbials of time (later, meanwhile, after a while), place (nearby, far away, beyond the wall), and number (secondly, finally, in addition) to guide the reader through a multi-paragraph text
evidence: Begin a new paragraph with an adverbial of time to signal a shift in time or sequence, e.g. 'Meanwhile, back at the castle...' or 'Several hours later, the storm finally passed'
Use adverbials of place to move the reader to a new location between paragraphs, e.g. 'Beyond the forest, the land was flat and dry'
Use numbering or addition adverbials to structure non-fiction across paragraphs, e.g. 'The first reason... The second reason... In addition...'

dependents.reason: Cross-paragraph linking extends KS2 linking ideas across paragraphs with adverbials

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Progressive and Continuous Tenses
topic.description: Form and use the progressive (continuous) verb tenses — past progressive (was walking), present progressive (am walking), and future progressive (will be walking) — to convey ongoing actions at different times
evidence: Write sentences using past progressive to describe an action that was ongoing at a particular time, e.g. 'She was reading when the phone rang'
Distinguish present progressive from simple present, e.g. 'I am eating lunch' (right now) vs 'I eat lunch at noon' (habitual)
Form the future progressive using 'will be' + present participle to describe an action that will be ongoing, e.g. 'Tomorrow at 3pm I will be travelling'

dependents.reason: Verb tense variety builds on progressive tenses

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Punctuating Titles of Works

Use quotation marks for titles of short works such as poems, songs, and articles

topic.name: Quoted and reported speech

evidence: Change '"I am tired," said Mia' into reported speech ('Mia said that she was tired')

topic.subject: English

evidence: Use the root-word clue for endings that sound like /ʃəs/: when the root word ends in -ce, the ending is usually -cious (space → spacious, grace → gracious, vice → vicious, malice → malicious); learn other -cious and -tious words (such as precious, cautious and ambitious) as words to know, noting exceptions such as anxious
Choose between -cial (usually after a vowel: special, official) and -tial (usually after a consonant: essential, partial) when spelling words with the /ʃəl/ ending

Choose -ant/-ance/-ancy or -ent/-ence/-ency using clues: -ent/-ence/-ency after a soft c, soft g or qu sound (innocent/innocence, intelligent, frequent/frequency); -ant/-ance/-ancy when a related word has a clear /æ/ or /eɪ/ sound, often an -ation word (observation → observant/observance, hesitation → hesitant/hesitancy); -ent/-ence when a related word has a clear /ɛ/ sound (confidential → confident/confidence); a hard c or g sound heard just before the ending can be a possible clue for -ant (significant, elegant); and learn the many words where no clue decides

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Similes in texts
topic.description: Recognise a simile — a figurative comparison that uses “like” or “as” to show that two unlike things share a quality — in a story, poem or other text that is read aloud or read independently; identify the two things being compared and the quality they share; and explain the picture, feeling or meaning the simile creates in that context. Ordinary uses of “like” or “as” that do not compare unlike things (“I like pizza”, “as soon as”, “she looks like her sister”) are not similes. Interpreting metaphors (implied comparisons with no “like” or “as”) and writing new figurative language are not part of this claim. The examples are illustrations, not a word list, a limit or a level.
evidence: In a story or poem they hear or read, find a simile and name the two unlike things being compared and the quality they share (e.g. in “the puppy’s fur was as soft as a cloud”: the fur and a cloud, both soft)
Explain what picture or feeling a simile creates and how it helps the reader understand the character, setting or event in that text (e.g. “he ran like the wind” shows how fast he was going)
Tell a simile apart from ordinary uses of “like” or “as” that do not compare unlike things (e.g. “I like pizza”, “as soon as I got home”, “she looks like her sister”) and explain the difference
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears “the puppy’s fur was as soft as a cloud” in a bedtime story, can they tell you which two things are being compared and what that tells you about the puppy?

prerequisites.reason: Noticing expressive and sensory phrases helps a child explain the picture a simile creates; optional — a child can explain that “ran like the wind” shows speed without having practised spotting recurring story language or choosing favourite phrases
prerequisites.name: Expressive and Sensory Language

topic.name: Writing Character & Dialogue
topic.description: Write narratives that develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique — including establishing context and point of view, developing characters through dialogue, pacing, and description, using varied transitions, and providing a reflective conclusion
evidence: Open a narrative by establishing setting, point of view, and a hook that engages the reader
Use dialogue, pacing, and descriptive detail to develop characters and advance the plot
Craft a conclusion that reflects on the narrated events rather than simply ending the action
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a story, do they use techniques like describing feelings, building suspense, or showing dialogue to make it interesting to read?

prerequisites.reason: KS3 narrative technique builds on KS2 planning narrative writing from author techniques
prerequisites.name: Planning Narratives

prerequisites.reason: Writing narratives with pacing, point of view, and varied transitions depends on command of the full toolkit of transitional and cohesive devices for signalling shifts in time, setting, and perspective
prerequisites.name: Cohesion and Transitions Across Writing

prerequisites.reason: KS3 narrative writing extends KS2 writing narratives with settings, characters, and plot
prerequisites.name: Narrative Writing

dependents.reason: Writing scripts and poetry builds on narrative writing techniques
dependents.name: Writing Across Genres

topic.subject: English
topic.name: Writing Techniques for Effect
topic.description: Apply growing knowledge of vocabulary, grammar, and text structure to writing — drawing on literary and rhetorical devices from reading (e.g., rhetorical questions, tricolon, anaphora, contrast) to enhance impact
evidence: Use a rhetorical question or tricolon deliberately in a persuasive piece and explain the intended effect
Employ varied sentence openings and structures to maintain reader interest across a whole piece
Draw on a literary device encountered in reading and apply it consciously in own writing
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} edits a piece of their writing, do they make choices about word order, sentence structure, or vocabulary to make the writing more powerful or clearer?

prerequisites.reason: Applying rhetorical devices (tricolon, anaphora, rhetorical questions) to enhance writing impact builds on the prior ability to write confidently for a wide range of purposes and forms beyond narrative
prerequisites.name: Writing Across Genres

prerequisites.reason: Using literary devices in writing requires recognising them in reading first
prerequisites.name: Figurative Language and Literary Devices

prerequisites.reason: Applying rhetorical devices extends KS2 choosing precise and vivid words
prerequisites.name: Vivid Word Choices

dependents.reason: Argument writing benefits from conscious application of rhetorical and literary devices drawn from reading — the student who can use tricolon or contrast intentionally will write more persuasive arguments
dependents.name: Persuasive Writing
